content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper address a fine-tuning process for overfitting the small downstream task, where the authors propose a parameter-efficient tuning process to overcome the drawbacks of full fine-tuning. The proposed method is named Important Channel Tuning (ICT), where the proposed module determines the most informative channels in the feature map for effective adaptation. Once the important channels are obtained they apply a linear layer for fine-tuning to the small downstream task.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- the paper is well written and extensive experiments are conducted to show the improvements of using the ICT module in Fine-tuning for the downstream task.
Weaknesses:
- Can the proposed valid for other types of networks that are not transformer-based like ResNet or U-Net. 
- will the same import tant channel concept can be applied to segmentation or restoration tasks?
- Supplementary table 12 experiments for different K values, for better performance K has to be higher i.e. K >=96 ( which is almost half of the channels), Can you explain more clearly why the significance of K in ICT performance since fine tuning half of the channels (k=96 where total channels are 192) can still be computationally expensive. 
- What is the significance of the Scale factor in Fig.3, can you show any experiment to understand better about scale factor?
- importance score is defined as the average of different categories of the channel (Eq.1), can authors clearly explain why the average is chosen? ( why not any other operation or learnable score function or target label dependent function)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper proposed a good fine-tuning process using an important channels-based module. This work can be easily implemented.
content.summary_of_the_review: Please weaknesses for detailed concerns, overall this is a good work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors present an observation investigating the statistics of the extracted feature maps from the frozen backbone and then design an importance score to reflect the importance of each channel. This paper proposes to choose the top-K largest value of importance score vectors and only update features of these channels with high importance scores. In this way, we can tune only a subset of channels instead of all, inheriting the strong representations of pre-trained backbones for downstream tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

S1. The method is intuitive and well-motivated.

S2. The design of the method is natural and very easy to understand.

S3. The experimental results are acceptable.

S4. The dataset-specific channel selection is conducted before downstream training and requires no more repeated channel selection computational cost. 

Weaknesses

W1. This paper is not very informative. The only take-home message is that the channels are not equally important to the transfer performance. It is good to point that out, but that is not very interesting or impressive.

W2. It is claimed in the abstract and introduction that transfer performance is critical to the downstream tasks but transfer results on downstream tasks like segmentation and object detection are not reported. I understand it is a common practice in the transfer learning community to conduct classification experiments only so I did not lower my rating for this. I just suggest the authors remove such claims since there is actually no experimental evidence.

W3. Some typos and ill-formulated formulas:
Page 3 bottom, criteria.
Page 4, Equation 2, use \text{Concat}, or it will be viewed as a product of C, o, n, c, a and t. There are many other similar cases.
Important score => importance score.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The method is about picking up channels important to finetuning, which is well-motivated and well-designed. The paper is well-written and easy to follow. Though the method and results are not very impressive, I see enough novelty in it as an ICLR paper. The experiments are conducted in standard settings so I am satisfied with the reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: As I commented in the Strengths & Weaknesses part, the quality of this paper is not very impressive but acceptable as an ICLR paper, so I rate it a borderline accept.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a parameter-efficient finetuning method that identifies, independently of the downstream task, a small fraction of the parameters to finetune. Competitive finetuning is demonstrated, comparing to methods that are less parameter efficient.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The proposed method is simple, effective (as demonstrated on the VTAB benchmark suite), and addresses an important problem of improving the target task performance without the need to store a separate finetuned model for each task. The experimental validation is given for a variety of visual tasks (VTAB), using several deep architectures.

I have a couple of concerns that limit the influence that this paper could have:

(1) It is unclear to me what precisely the paper is doing, partly because some of the described interventions are not mathematically defined.

- How is the identified set of important channels used? There is figure 3, as well as some of the text descriptions in the beginning of sec. 3.3, but I could not find any equations or code that tell me how the features are used, or what is the linear layer that is used or how it is is introduced into the model.

- In Eq. (2), it says that Concat concatenates after L2 normalization -- I did not understand this. Could the normalization be written explicitly? As written, I interpret (2) as being a vector of squared L2 norms.

- I didn't understand why Eq. (1) gives a class-aware importance score. It appears to average per-class average squared norms of features, so would this not be simply the same as average feature norms? In other words, could we not just average over all examples, rather than doing nested averaging over examples within each class and then over all classes?

(2) What is the rationale for the proposed method? Why are the channels with large activations those that are best to fine-tune? I think it is important to justify this choice, in addition to the empirical evidence that the paper provides. The paper does show empirically that (on a particular problem and model architecture, at least) the norms of different channels differ. From this, the paper infers that some channels are more important than others. However,

- Does a larger norm indicate that the feature is indeed more important? Could the larger norm not correspond to smaller weights attached to the feature? The paper's conclusion implies that the performance of the model on different tasks varies more in the subspace of the larger-norm features than the others -- why is this the case?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The method seems novel (but I am not well versed in the related art) and the empirical evidence is strong, but the paper does not clearly describe what is done, or why.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposed a simple method for identifying a small fraction of the parameters to finetune, and shows empirically that this method fares well vs. the competitors. However the paper is not clearly describing what the method is, and does not seem to offer a clear justification for the choices that are made, nor a clear explanation for the observed phenomena.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a parameter-efficient tuning method called Important Channel Tuning (ICT). To this end, ICT first identifies the most informative channels from the feature maps and then only tunes those channels using the Important Channel Tuning Module (ICTM). Experiments on VTAB-1K benchmark show that the proposed ICT with fewer additional parameters achieves better performance than the full fine-tuning method in most cases. However, the motivation and some important details are unclear. Please see my detailed comments.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: The proposed method is simple yet effective. The proposed method is able to achieve better performance than the full fine-tuning method while only introducing a small number of parameters. 

Questions and points needed to be improved:

1.	Some notations are confusing. For example, in Section 3.2, what does N^K denote? Please provide more explanations.

2.	The motivation for the proposed class-aware importance score is unclear. Why do important channels have large features norm? It would be better for the authors to provide more explanations, which would strengthen the paper.

3.	In Section 3.3, the proposed method introduces an additional full-connected layer to tune the informative channels. Why not directly tune the weight corresponding to the informative channels?

4.	Some important details are missing. For example, in Section 3.3, the proposed method introduces additional scaling to determine the weights of different branches of features. However, how to determine the value of scaling? It would be better for the authors to provide more experiments.

5.	In Figure 5, it would be better for the authors to show the average accuracy of Full, Linear and Bias on natural, specialized and structured tasks, which helps to give  comprehensive performance comparisons between different methods.

6.	In Section 4.1, what does Linear denote? Only tuning the last full-connected layer?

7.	In Table 3, what does w/o CA denote, using the entire training set?

content.title: Important Channel Tuning
content.abstract: Large vision transformers (ViT) have tremendously succeeded in various computer vision tasks. These ViT models pre-trained on large datasets such as ImageNet21K and JFT-300M enjoy robustness in both low-level and high-level visual representations, and they repeatedly yield performance improvements on multiple downstream tasks. One straightforward way to inherit these robust representations is full fine-tuning. However, full fine-tuning is prone to overfitting the small downstream data by adjusting the massive weights of pre-trained large models. In addition, updating the whole parameters of pre-trained large models requires high GPU memory and computations, which limits the application of these large models. To address the above two drawbacks of full fine-tuning, in this paper, we propose a parameter-efficient tuning (PET) method dubbed Important Channel Tuning (ICT). Different from previous PET methods that adopt a trainable module to tune all the channels of a feature map, we hypothesize and corroborate experimentally that not all channels are equal for adaptation. Specifically, we design a tiny external module that determines the most informative channels in the feature map for effective adaptation. In particular, with only a simple linear layer applied to the important channels, our ICT surpasses full fine-tuning on 18 out of 19 datasets in VTAB-1K benchmark by adding only 0.11M parameters of the ViT-B, which is 0.13% of its full fine-tuning counterpart. Moreover, compared with the previous PET methods, ICT achieves the state-of-the-art average performance in the VTAB-1K benchmark with ViT and Swin Transformer backbones.
